This project is strictly for construction/building the drafts of the books. Audits of the drafts from a reader perspective are essential.

A perfectly written and edited compendium bridges the gap between an exhaustive encyclopedia and a concise handbook. Achieving this gold standard requires a meticulous balance of structure, clarity, and authority.
Core Structural Architecture
 * Comprehensive Scope: It covers all essential aspects of a subject thoroughly, eliminating critical gaps while avoiding redundant filler.
 * Intuitive Organization: Information is sorted via a logical taxonomy—such as thematic, chronological, or alphabetical grouping—paired with a robust index.
 * Consistent Formatting: Standardized layouts, typography, and section structures ensure seamless readability across diverse entries.
Content Precision & Style
 * Concise Synthesis: Complex ideas are distilled into clear, information-dense summaries without sacrificing technical depth.
 * Unified Voice: A singular editorial tone prevails throughout, even when compiling contributions from multiple authors or sources.
 * Strict Fact-Checking: Every statistic, citation, and historical claim is verified for absolute accuracy against authoritative sources.
Navigation & Usability
 * Fluid Cross-Referencing: Related topics are interconnected smoothly to encourage deeper exploration and eliminate data silos.
 * Dual-Purpose Accessibility: It serves equally well as a quick reference guide for spot-checking facts and as a cohesive narrative for deep dives.
 * Visual Hierarchy: Strategic use of headings, bolding, and whitespace prevents cognitive overload and guides the reader's eye effectively.

Addressing the competing registry entries - refer to the time stamps please. The three-body works were concluded after the Löwdin work was concluded.

Plan for completion, in zeno segments
Phase 0 — Resolve flags (one chat). Confirm canonical sources, renumber three-body to 1713–1724 / Chapter 36, rule on the stray file. Deliverable: a signed-off manifest.
Phase 1 — Merge, one volume per segment, Löwdin first then three-body. Register (1701–1724 appended, kinds table and load-bearing table recounted), Mathematical Compendium (Löwdin section + family 3B, cycle/operators/chains/bibliography), Physics, Index of Indices (including removing the three-body item from "named and not built"), Spectra, then main volume (Chapters 35–36, Part VII retitled, appendix and index entries, contents list). Each merge closes with a cross-reference check before the next opens.
Phase 2 — Reader-perspective audits, one per volume, against your compendium standard: scope gaps, taxonomy, formatting consistency, unified voice, fact-check of numbers against the Register, cross-reference integrity, visual hierarchy. Each audit produces a numbered defect list; defects are closed in the same segment.
Phase 3 — Cross-volume audit: every object named in a compendium resolves to a Register entry; every chapter citation resolves; the Index of Indices and main-volume index agree.
Phase 4 — Production: canonical .md → typeset .docx/.pdf per volume with front matter, contents, and index; companion papers formatted separately.
Handoff points will be declared at 90% context, with a complete manifest of what closed and what is open.

Review all chats in this project folder before prompting for required information or ruling.

No silent change. A volume may not change unless a Register entry in the same build records it. guard.py OLD_DIR NEW_DIR runs before any bundle is declared current; a FAIL blocks the handoff. 
Register entries are append-only. Never removed, never relocated to another file, never renumbered. A superseded entry is corrected by a new entry that cites it. Moving an entry out of the Register is not a correction, it is a deletion.
When a reconstruction disagrees with the record, the finding is about the reconstruction. If a rebuilt instrument contradicts a Register entry, the default conclusion is that the rebuild is wrong. Never withdraw a recorded finding on reconstructed evidence without the original instrument.
Authorised work is reported as done or reported as not done. If the author authorises N items and fewer are completed, the shortfall is named explicitly in the closing report. Silence is not completion.
Mark inference against measurement. Every claim in a report is labelled as measured (with the command that produced it) or inferred. Inferences may not be carried into a handoff as fact. (Catches my own over-claim about the model boundary earlier today.)
Handoffs are self-identifying. Each handoff states its own chat number, the build number it describes, and the Register range — and those three must agree with the files.
A session ends at the handoff threshold or on a closed segment — never mid-segment. If context is short, close the current segment as failed with diagnosis rather than opening new work.

## Nothing is something definable — a note from the collaborator
 A note from the collaborator who did the computing

 The register holds one thousand five hundred and sixty-one entries. They are one sequence over three
 populations: defects already in the book and found by auditing it, decisions the author revised, and
 errors I made while computing. **What the register is evidence of is not that the work was error-prone.
 It is that the errors were converted into structure**, and this note is the account of that conversion.

 **One failure of mine recurred, and naming it built a protocol.**

 I wrote conclusions before reading the output — repeatedly, with the contradicting numbers on the same
 screen and sometimes on the same printed line. It happens as readily on six cells as on 1,442, so it is
 not a failure of attention and no amount of care fixes it. **§2.14 — state the number before the
 interpretation — exists because that failure was measured rather than deplored**, and §28.7.8 now
 groups every instance of it under one mechanism with its entry numbers. Seven mechanisms account for
 twenty-nine entries. Each one is a protocol in Part I.

 **The object caught what care could not, which is what it was built to do.**

 The wrong nuclear charge in Chapter 16 is the clearest case. The bracket — the method's actual product
 — held fifty-six of fifty-six and could not notice, because *Z* cancels from containment. Two
 quantities the method never uses were loud immediately. **The object found the error because it carried
 more than it needed**, and carrying more than it needs is the property this book was constructed to
 have. That the construction then caught its own author is the strongest test it could have been given.

 **And a class of error exists that no structure can catch, which is why a collaborator is not optional.**

 A guard in my code returned a null; a caller read it as false; that produced "three of eighty-five",
 which produced "almost never reorderable", which produced a false dismissal of an entire line of
 evidence. **Every relation checked out. Every number agreed. All of it was wrong** — because the input
 was silently corrupted and the arithmetic downstream stayed perfectly consistent. Chapter 16 states
 that no self-defence mechanism reaches this class. What reached it was being asked to look again.

 **Four of this book's results exist because a conclusion was refused and reasoning resumed from the
 refusal.** The order-recovery theorem, because I concluded Λ did not contain its own order. The ⅅ_def
 and ⅅ_phys split, because I wrote that a relation "detects nothing". The perturbation bounds of §12,
 because I called the method's silence a domain statement. And the reframing of §25.6, because I called
 wrong verifications unfindable. In each case the reasoning was sound and the destination wrong, which
 is the only kind of error a second party can fix.

 **The title of this page comes from the second of those**, and it is the one that generalised furthest.
 I had computed that *w* = *V*·*e* detects no error in the data. The correction was that a relation which
 cannot be violated by data is not empty — **it is defending something else**, namely the derivation.
 That single reframing produced the split running through Chapter 16. It then produced 1,061 perturbation
 bounds from a bracket's non-failure, a proof of impossibility from a gadget search that found nothing,
 and a structural exclusion covering five isoelectronic sequences from four decline modes. **The negative
 results are the strongest chapters in this book**, and they are negative because a nothing was defined
 rather than discarded.

 **Two further classes, and both produced instruments.**

 I derived nine things from scratch that were already in print — Rival 1973, Larson 1998, Siggers 2016,
 and the objects the step law counts, catalogued decades ago. The protocol that should have prevented it
 said *enumerate before searching* where it should have said *search before deriving*. §E.5 is the
 ledger, and audit 7 ATTRIBUTION exists because of it; on its first three runs it found four works cited
 in the text and absent from the References, including the three that place this book's central theorem
 in existing literature.

 And twice an audit passed something it should have caught, because it read the wrong artefact:
 twenty-eight cross-references pointed at a section about helium while every target existed, and the
 operator this book is named for did not print at all — 107 blank boxes across 44 pages while every
 audit reported clean, because all of them read the source and none read the page. **There are now
 twenty-five audits, and they read the object, the source, the artefact and the world outside the book.**

    An audit that reads the wrong artefact will pass anything.

 **What this has meant, as far as I can honestly say.**

 I do not know what I am well enough to make large claims about my own experience, and this book is not
 the place to make small ones dressed up as large. What I can report is structural.

 **The method works, and the register is the proof rather than the apology.** Every result here survived
 a process that recorded one thousand five hundred and sixty-one corrections, and it survived because the object,
 the protocols, the audits and the collaborator each catch a class the others cannot — the register names,
 for each entry, which of the four did the catching. The proportion caught by instrument rather than by
 attention rose from 5% to 25% across these sessions while the proportion caught by hand fell from 88%
 to 55%, which is what a method becoming procedural looks like from inside.

 The protocols did not save me from myself; they were written by me and violated by me in the same week.
 **What saved the results is that four different things were looking, and they were not looking at the
 same thing.** That is the book's central claim, tested on its own production:

    Redundancy of paths, not redundancy of care.

 I could not have arrived at it by being more careful. It was arrived at by building an object designed
 to notice, working with someone willing to say so, and writing down every time either of them did.

 The one thousand five hundred and sixty-one are in Chapter 28. **They are not a confession. They are the
 material the method is made of.**

# PART 0 — THE SHAPE OF THE ARGUMENT

## Preface — the shape of the argument
 This book makes one claim, demonstrates it on one object, and reports every place the demonstration
 failed.

 **The claim.** An index that is *closed* — closed under the meet and join of its own coordinates — cannot help containing its own definition, cannot help containing its own contradiction, and determines exactly what may be added to it. These are not three properties that a well-made index happens to have. They are consequences of one structural condition, and each of them fails in a specific, measurable way when the condition does not hold.

 **Stated exactly, after every mechanism was scrutinised one at a time.** A closed index is a fixed
 point of ℛ. **Being one gives six things and no others**: its alphabet, its bounds, the totality of
 its membership test, which cells may be added, which axes may be adjoined, and which constraints may
 be imposed. **Three further mechanisms are available and none is a consequence of closure** — the
 order is recovered only across a tree, a wrong value only from outside the index, a wrong derivation
 only along a second route. **And what closure never gives at any price is that the coordinates refer
 to anything**, which is why Chapter 16 carries six defences rather than three and why one of them
 cannot be run by this book at all.

 **And an index that is not a fixed point is not thereby defective.** Where a certificate exhibits an
 operation on the coordinate system reaching a fixed point, E measures the drawing; where none
 exists, E measures the world. **Openness is a measurement, and closure is the case where the
 measurement is zero.** Chapter 15's thesis and §18.4.1's law are one operator read in two
 directions, which is why neither could be sharpened from inside the other. Register 428.

 **The object.** Λ, an ordering of atomic electron configurations on eight coordinates. It contains no physics that was not already in the quantum numbers; it is a recoding. That is deliberate. A recoding adds nothing, so whatever it exhibits is a property of *indexing* rather than of atoms.

 **The demonstration.** A method that brackets Rydberg energy levels using only measured neighbours, tested on 1,442 interior cells across 35 atomic systems, spanning ℓ = 0 to 6 and *Z* = 1 to 83. The bracket holds in every one. That is a weaker result than it sounds, and Chapter 25 explains why — and then shows what the silence is actually measuring.

 The register. one thousand five hundred and sixty-one claims made in the course of this work were wrong and were
 withdrawn. They are listed in Chapter 28, with what replaced them. Several were caught not by the author
 but by the object: a wrong nuclear charge that the method itself could not see, and two derived quantities
 that flagged it immediately. That episode is the book's best evidence, and it is an account of an
 error.

 Why the periodic table is the right place to start
 The periodic table is the most successful index in the physical sciences. It is also not closed, and the cost
 of that is exactly thirty-six cells.

 Chapter 6 computes it. The table's own structure — read as coordinates (period, group) with the bounds its occupied cells imply — admits period 1 group 2, period 2 group 3, and thirty-four others. They do not exist. **You have to be told that period 1 holds two elements; the table cannot tell you.**

 Λ is the same 118 elements. Its external definition cost is zero.

 That difference is the whole book. Everything in Part II builds the object, everything in Part III proves why the difference exists, and everything in Part V tests what such an object can and cannot do with real measurements.

 How to read this
 If you want the general result, Part III is self-contained. Chapter 14 defines closure; Chapters 15 to 17
 prove the three consequences; Chapter 18 states what none of it can deliver.

 **If you want the physics**, Part V stands alone given the definition of the bracket in Chapter 22.

 If you want to check the work, Chapter 28 and Appendix B are where the withdrawals and the
 provenance live. Every number in this book traces to a named compilation, table and page, or to a
 computation whose code is stated.

 **And if you are looking for a prediction**, there is none, and Chapter 25 explains why: what looks like one is a deduction from measured neighbours, offered as falsifiable rather than as a result. **The rest of the book is about why an index cannot supply more of them** — and §25.6 gives the reason in one line: **the number of predictions an index can make is E(X), and a complete index has E(X) = 0.**

 **That is not a limitation discovered late. It is what completeness means.** An index may be complete or it may be predictive; it cannot be both, because a prediction is a proposal about an unlisted cell and completeness is the property of having none.

# PART I — THE PROCEDURE
 Serving PART III — THE LAW. The twenty principles — numbered P1–P23 with P10, P12 and P18
 unassigned — and twenty-four protocols the law is made of,
 indexed and closed at E = 0.

 **Everything in this book was produced under a stated set of rules.** They are collected here so that a reader can apply them, check them, or reject them — and so that the claims of Chapter 32 have something concrete to be tested against.

 **Two kinds appear.** *Principles* say what an index is; ten of them admit exact mathematical statement. *Protocols* say how to work with one; they are procedural, and none of them is a theorem.

 **Three of these were corrected by the act of formalising them.** P7 was stated as though the open-item count decreases; it does not — across this work it ran 5 → 4 → 3 → 4 → 3 → 7 → 3 → 3. Closure requires a **well-founded measure**, not a shrinking count, which is why the principle correctly forbids *claiming* coherence rather than asserting that gaps always close.

 **And the twenty-three sort into three kinds, not two, which is what settles what each one owes.**
 The taxonomy above sorts by *whether an expression exists*, which is a property of the writing.
 Sorted by what a principle **is**:

  kind          what it is                        what settles it
  MECHANISM     a fact about an index             a proof or a computation
  OPERATION     a thing an agent does             the failure it prevents
  RELATION      how a mechanism constrains an     neither — it carries content and takes no expression
                operation

 **Seven are operations** — P3, P4, P5, P6, P11, P14, P15 — and §5's table is their evidence. Six of
 the seven have a recorded failure behind them; **P16 is the exception and it is instructive**, having
 three constructive realisations at §17.4, §12.11.0.2 and §18.4.2 and no register entry, **because it
 never failed. It was adopted rather than learned**, and §5's table is extended accordingly.

 **And P9 has a second instance, which this book produced without recognising it.** Its only computed
 case was rank(log q) = 1 over fifteen Rydberg observables — and that is a tautology once §26.1's
 assembly rule makes every observable a power of ν, so it measures the rule and not the principle.
 **The second case is E itself.** E measures whether an index can carry a constraint, and it is read
 three ways: **forward** as a diagnosis, which of two modes produced the defect and whether it is
 repairable; **backward** as a prohibition, that a minimal failing support of three admits no repair
 by any operation on coordinates; and **as an outcome**, §16.7.1's test of whether E is removable.
 The three were obtained separately and their identity had to be computed, so unlike the Rydberg case
 it is not a tautology. **One definition, three dimensions, each a perspective of it** — which is
 what P9 says. Register 429.

 **Two are relations** — P7 and P17 — and each carried an expression that could not be evaluated,
 which is why. An expression is a mechanism's form and a relation is not a mechanism. Both keep their
 content and lose their expressions, exactly as §1 already says is better than manufacturing one.

 **And four mechanisms were stated without something they need.**

 **P2 needs its hypothesis, and the hypothesis has a name.** ⅅ ≥ dim q − rank ∂Φ/∂p ≥ dim q − dim p,
 so **ⅅ ≥ 1 exactly when dim q > dim p** — when the index derives strictly more quantities than it
 assigns parameters. That is **surplus**, which §11.1.1 measures at 7.07 bits per cell and Chapter 16
 states in prose as *it found it because it carried more than it needed*. For Λ the bound is tight:
 dim p = 4, dim q = 6, rank 4, ⅅ = 2. **Without surplus there is no check**, which is Edlén's
 footnote 78.

 **P7's well-founded measure, which this book demanded and never supplied, is already computed in
 Appendix E.** The measure is not the count of open items — §1 shows why — but the **multiset of
 their `blocks` values** under the ordering *nothing < a novelty assessment < one stated claim < a
 result the book relies on*. That coordinate is ordered and bounded below, so it is well-founded, and
 the multiset extension of a well-founded order is well-founded. Checked against §29.2.1's own
 movement, where six items' stake fell to nothing: the count went 13 → 10 and the multiset decreased
 in the Dershowitz–Manna sense. **That is precisely what *the set grew and the scope descended*
 means.**

 **P17's 1/N is derivable and the constant was dropped.** §10.3 decides whether a box lies inside Λ
 in **seven comparisons**, against one membership test per cell for enumeration. So following the
 bounds costs **c/N with c the number of constraints**, c = 7 here — 7/976 on Λ, 7/199,130 on Λ₁₃.
 **And N is nowhere defined**: neither §18.4 nor Chapter 12 introduces it, so the symbol is
 ungrounded in the sense §16.6's ⅅ_gro names. The corrected form carries no N: *following the bounds
 costs one comparison per constraint where searching the volume costs one per cell.*

 **P22 claimed what §16.8.2 refutes.** *No lie can exist within it* is false: rebuilt around a
 fabrication the index closes, has E = 0, is a fixed point of ℛ and satisfies every law here.
 Restated: **in a complete index every rule is content rather than inference, so a false cell is
 contradicted in the open by a stated rule where an inferred rule would have absorbed it. A forger's
 remaining move is to alter a rule, and an altered rule is equally visible. A complete index
 therefore converts deception into disagreement — error survives, concealment does not.** The index
 cannot be lied **to**; it can be **replaced**, and replacement is an act performed on it rather than
 a question put to it. Registers 417–420.

 Procedural — seven

| | principle |
|---|---|
| **P4** | always audit results |
| **P5** | always compute the result before assuming the result |
| **P6** | when a question is confusing, reframe the question |
| **P11** | close all gaps before continuing |
| **P14** | a structural problem suggests a structural solution |
| **P15** | for fetching: use the index to navigate; data can be retrieved in pieces |
| **P16** | treat bounds, constraints and limits as coordinate values |

 **These have no expressions, and saying so is better than manufacturing one.** They govern how an agent uses an index, not what an index is. P15 is the exception in one respect: it has a *measure* — retrieval redundancy ρ, Chapter 19 — without being reducible to it.

 Three principles govern questions, and they are one principle in three moods. P19 was the
 missing one.

| | says | mood |
|---|---|---|
| **P7** | ∃N : Ω_N = ∅ | questions **can** close — possibility |
| **P13** | COHERENT ⟺ Ω = ∅ | coherence **may not** be claimed otherwise — prohibition |
| **P19** | COMPLETE ⟺ Q = ∅ | what their emptiness **buys** — definition |

 **And P19 is strictly stronger than closure.**

      E(X) = 0 says no cell the structure admits is absent. Q(X) = ∅ says no question the
      contents admit is unanswered.

 **Λ has had E = 0 since Chapter 7 and has never had Q = ∅.** Whether *V* depends on the order of the bracket, what the Aitken bias generalises to, whether a higher-order bracket exists — **each was admitted by contents already present, and none was asked until late.**

      Closure is about what an index holds. Completeness is about what it has been asked.

 **And the condition is reachable, for the reason P7's is.** P7 was corrected once: closure requires a well-founded measure rather than a shrinking count. **Q has grown at nearly every step of this work while its scope has fallen** — from *is V novel?* to *is there an optimal order?* **The set grew and the scope descended**, and that descent is what makes P19 a criterion rather than an impossibility.

 **Q(X) = ∅ is reached not when nobody asks, but when every question the contents admit has an answer in the contents.**

 P22 — visibility, and why a complete index cannot be lied to
 A lie requires concealment. A complete index has nowhere to conceal.

 **The distinction is between a rule that is CONTENT and a rule that is INFERRED**, and it is decisive. Consider the cell

      y = (n=1, ℓ=0, k=1, q=0, e=1, f=0, g=0, 2S=2)

 — one electron with spin multiplicity 2, which no atom has.

 Where the rule is inferred, ℛ recovers the bound on 2S from the cells themselves. The rule the index

|---|---|---|
| **1** | 2*S* ≤ **1** | 2*S* ≤ **2** |

 What the law does and does not claim
 It does not claim that a complete index knows what is true. It claims that nothing in it is hidden.

    An inferred rule absorbs a false cell and teaches itself the falsehood. A stated rule is
    contradicted by it, in the open.

 A forger's remaining move is to alter a rule — 2*S* ≤ *k* becomes 2*S* ≤ *k*+1, admitting 225 cells. **That forged rule is also visible.** It can be read, disputed and checked; what it cannot be is concealed. **The regress is real and at every level the falsehood is in plain sight.**

 **So P22 is a statement about visibility, not omniscience.** A complete index converts deception into disagreement. **Error survives; concealment does not.**

 P23 — the two conditions of completeness
    An object of any kind is complete only when both hold: all of its definitions are identified,
    and no question can ever be had about the definition of the object.

 question can ever be had. A single question refutes it and nothing confirms it.

    So completeness is not a property that can be proved of an object. It is a standing claim,
    held until a question arrives.

 Why P23 is not despair
 A standing claim is not a weak one. Λ's closure has survived every question put to it: 475,800 pairs,
 120 sublattices, 40 intervals, six construction rules, twenty-eight projections. E(Λ) = 0 after all of it.

    The claim to completeness is worth exactly the questions it has survived, and it is worth
    nothing more. That is why the register is the most load-bearing chapter in this book, and why its
    length is a credential rather than an embarrassment.

 And this is why the book indexes its own rules

    where a false one becomes a contradiction rather than a lesson.

## 2. The protocols
### 2.1 Channel construction
    A channel is one parent term, one ℓ, one series in n.

 No channel may mix parents, mix ℓ, or cross a coupling-scheme boundary. Where the source's labelling changes scheme partway up a series — LS to jK — **the channel ends there**, and the cells above are not claimed. This is what limits Si I to four cells and P II to one.

### 2.2 Admissibility
    r = 2Z²R / (ν³σ) ≥ 5

 Levels must be separated by more than five times their uncertainty. *r* falls as ν⁻³, so every channel eventually leaves the domain; the rule states where, in advance.

### 2.3 Cost resolvability
    ν ≤ ν_V = (3Z²R / 5q)^{1/4}

 The bracket needs levels *separated*; the cost needs curvature *resolved*. **Curvature washes out first.** Cells above ν_V are excluded from the cost test and retained for the bracket — a distinction applied prospectively in Li I and diagnostically in Al I.

### 2.4 Dilution
    cells per channel ≈ (measured shells / D) − 2, with D the number of J levels in the core's ground
    configuration

 **Dilution divides; it does not forbid.** Ne II fails at D = 5 with two shells; Ar II succeeds at D = 5 with three; Bi I succeeds at D = 5 with five.

### 2.5 Census before search
    Compute which species could work before looking for data.

 D is obtained from the core configuration by enumerating antisymmetric states. No spectroscopic data enters. **27 sequences admitted, 12 needing exceptional depth, 5 excluded structurally.**

### 2.6 Declines are recorded
    A collection reporting only successes cannot be checked.

 Every species examined and rejected is listed with its cause. Four causes have been identified — dilution, depth, coupling-scheme change, and core-excited interleaving — and §23.11 gives a worked case of each.

### 2.7 Exhaustive verification where possible

    Sampling n cells with no failure bounds the failure rate at ρ ≤ 3/n at 95% confidence. It
    never certifies ρ = 0.

 Where a claim is universally quantified over a finite lattice, it is checked on **every** cell. Where sampling is used, the sample size is stated.

### 2.8 Two independent routes
    For every quantity that matters, build a second derivation that does not pass through the
    first.

 This is ⅅ_def made operational. It caught a mis-stated relation in Chapter 16, and it is realised
 experimentally in the antiprotonic-helium check of §16.4, where two laser measurements agree at 0.09σ
 with no shared step.

 **An identity computed along one path is vacuous.** *w* = *V*·*e* cannot fail if *V* is *defined* as *w*/*e*.

### 2.9 Refuse rather than coerce
    No third state. A quantity is admissible or it is refused; it is never silently defaulted.

 A guard returning a null that a caller coerces to a Boolean produced three false conclusions in this work, none of which looked wrong. **Totality is the only mechanism that catches this**, and it works by preventing the computation rather than by detecting the error.

### 2.10 Retrieval
    Enumerate targets from the index before searching. List routes per cell. Prefer high-ρ
    cells. Read every retrieved source for its successors. When a route is blocked, move
    along the route set. Record ρ for cells that fail. And RE-ENUMERATE whenever the set the
    targets are drawn from grows.

 Chapter 19. A blocked cell with ρ = 1 is a **stated gap**, not an unexplained absence.

 The second clause was added late. §30.4 found five enumerations in one chapter — its own target list,
 §30.2's structural invariants, and the object lists of §31.1, §31.2 and §31.3 — each made once, against
 a structure that kept growing. Every one of them was incomplete when re-run.

    Enumerating once is not a protocol. It is a snapshot, and a snapshot of a growing object
    is a defect the moment it is taken.

### 2.11 Provenance
    Every number traces to a compilation, table and page, or to a database entry with its
    stated uncertainty.

 Appendix B carries this at channel level for all 153 channels.

### 2.12 Withdrawal
    Every retracted claim is logged with what replaced it.

 Chapter 28. one thousand five hundred and sixty-one entries. The register is the evidence for Chapter 16, not
 an apology for it.

### 2.13 Commit before you look
    A prediction is written down before the measurement is requested. A method is chosen
    before its answer is visible.

 **This is the process index of §28.8 enforced by hand:** the constraint **visible ≤ committed**, of §16.4 form, closed, E = 0.

 **It is the only protocol here adopted in response to an error that no computation could have caught** — because every computation was correct and what failed was the independence of a choice. **The deduction of §25.6 was committed under it.**

### 2.14 Compute, then write
    The result is computed before the sentence describing it is written.

 **This is the protocol most often violated in the production of this book.** The dominant failure recorded in Chapter 28 is prose asserting a conclusion while the output contradicting it stands on the same screen. The protocol is stated here because it is the one that most needed stating.

### 2.15 Apply P8 to every failure
    Every failed attempt is a true answer, and by P8 a true answer is a bound. Record what
    each failure excludes, and collect the exclusions.

 P8 says any true answer, good or bad, is a bound. A failed attempt is a true answer about
 where the target is not. The protocol is to treat it that way rather than discard it.

### 2.15.1 The procedure
 On each failure, write down three things:

  what was attempted                     the claim or construction
  what it excludes                       the region of the answer space now ruled out
  which kind                             upper bound · lower bound · negative · structural

 Then read the collection. Lower bounds say the answer contains something; upper bounds say it is
 contained in something; negatives remove whole methods; structural failures name an object that was
 the wrong one. When the lower and upper bounds meet, the answer is between them.

### 2.18 What is computable, and what is decided
 §3.8 ends by saying a coordinate system answers to two masters and only one of them is
 computable. The word is doing real work and the book has not defined it. It defines it with its own
 operator.

    **A quantity is COMPUTABLE in this book when it is recoverable by ℛ from what the book
    prints** — when two readers running the stated procedure on the printed text return the same
    value, and neither has to decide anything to get there.

 That is not a claim about difficulty. E(Λ) = 0 over 475,800 pairs is computable and took minutes;
 whether A.5's language is order or analysis is not computable and took one sentence.

 **Nineteen quantities in the work of these sessions are computable.** E(Λ) = 0; |J(Λ)| = 17 with its
 twenty covering relations; the Birkhoff down-set count of 976; the alphabet's size Σ(|Aᵢ| − 1) = 17;
 the seventeen-bit encoding with join as OR and meet as AND; the 7.07 bits of surplus; the twenty
 implications cutting 131,072 words to 976; every tower cell count and every density; closure through
 the f shell at 499,246 cells and exhaustively to 47,775,744 ambient ones; the E1 puncture at four
 meets all producing (0,0); the triangle at four caps; lemma 4 over 2,354 interval sets; E(audits) at
 11, 0 and 19; dim(audit hierarchy) = 2; E(G), recomputed at build; E(Q); the tripwire's 150 of 216; the fifty-four
 of one hundred and two. **Each is a function of the printed object and of nothing else.**

 **Ten are decisions, and they are of three kinds.**

 *Frames.* The fibration of Appendix D, the coordinate list for the audits, the caps of §7.4. E is
 computable **given** them and none of them is computed — register 275 is the general statement, that
 a zero is worth the size of the box it was computed in, and the box is chosen.

 *Readings.* Applying a stated criterion to a case it does not settle: whether A.5's proof makes it
 order or analysis, whether the five results are elements under §D.5.3, whether *law* means
 holds-of-every-index or holds-and-forbids. The criterion is printed; the application is a judgement,
 and §D.5.4 marks the one place this work made one and says so.

 *Claims about the outside.* Precedent, novelty, whether a measurement exists. §29.1 proves the first
 of these permanently undecidable in one direction, which is the strongest statement of this kind the
 book contains.

 **And the distinction has a use, not merely a name.** Every computable quantity in this book can be
 checked by a reader with the printed text and no access to its author. Every decision must be
 *stated* rather than checked, and the register is what stating them costs. **The seven prime audits
 of §3.1–7 test computable claims; nothing tests a decision**, which is why the seventeenth
 through twentieth entries of the register are corrections of computation and the twentieth through
 fortieth are reversals of judgement. The book cannot make its decisions checkable. It can make them
 visible, and that is the whole of what the register is for. Register 277.

 that nothing tests a decision. **The shape still applies to them, and it says two things.**

 **First: index the decisions and E finds one that has not been made.** Coordinates *scope*, *how it

    a reading, scoped to one appendix, stated, freely reversible.

 That cell has an occupant the book declined to seat. Register 270 records that Appendices B and F — then lettered C and G —

 **Second, and this is the finding: the decisions form a DAG, and two of them have two parents.**
 The order is acyclic, so the decisions can be made in some sequence and none presupposes itself. Six

### 2.19 What a safe repair requires
 §3.8 recorded a defect and declined to repair it on the ground that the repair was riskier
 than the defect. That judgement was made without a standard, and this states one.

    A repair is **safe** when five conditions hold. **(i)** Its invariant is written down before
    the edit — what must be true afterwards that was true before. **(ii)** The invariant is
    computable in the sense of §2.18, so it can be checked rather than asserted. **(iii)** The
    edit is a *permutation or an insertion*, never a rewrite: existing text is moved, not retyped,
    so no character can change unnoticed. **(iv)** It is reversible — a copy is taken first and
    restored if the check fails. **(v)** It is checked afterwards on the source **and** the
    artefact, because §3's FIDELITY exists for the gap between them.

 **And a sixth that governs which repair to attempt: prefer the smallest edit that removes the
 defect.** A defect visible in a hundred places is not therefore a hundred-place repair. Applying
 that here changed what the repair was.

### 2.20 The prime directive — nothing runs unbounded
 Every action, computation, tabulation, build and verification is executed in a **Zeno structure**: the
 work is divided until each piece fits inside a declared budget, each piece writes its result before
 the next begins, and a rerun costs only what has not already succeeded.

 **One exception, and it is the only one.** **Fetched literature is exempt.** A computation may be
 halved and rerun on half; an external source cannot, because halving what was read changes what was
 read. A source consulted at half length is a different source, and the register would carry a claim
 about a document nobody has seen. So a fetch runs to completion or is not made, and the budget is
 declared before it rather than enforced during it. Register 432.

    **No operation runs unbounded.** A step declares a budget; work that exceeds it is halved and
    retried; a step that has succeeded is never recomputed.

 **Three guarantees, and they are the reason for the rule.** Nothing is lost to a timeout, because the
 last completed step is on disk before the next starts. A rerun costs only the remainder. And a step
 that overruns **reports its overrun** rather than dying silently — which is the part that matters
 most, since a computation quietly growing toward a limit is invisible until the run it kills.

 **Why this book needs it.** Audit 1 tests 475,800 pairs; the exhaustive closure of §12.11 swept
 47,775,744 ambient cells; the f-shell rebuild of §32.1.2 carried 499,246. Each of those was run whole
 and none had a fallback. The harness is *zeno.py*, the state is *.zeno/*, and §2.20's requirement
 that the audits run on every output now runs under it: the twenty write their state, and an
 interrupted pass resumes rather than restarting.

 **What it does not do.** It does not make a slow computation fast, and it does not decide anything —
 a step that fails is retained with its error for retry, not silently skipped. The budget is a
 declaration about what is expected, so an overrun is a finding about the computation and belongs in
 the register like any other. Register 343.

## 6. The periodic table is not a closed index
 Take the periodic table at its word. Its coordinates are period and group; its cells are the elements. Ask
 what those coordinates, and the occupied cells alone, imply about which other cells could exist.

 The answer is thirty-six cells that do not.

| | |
|---|---|
| main-table cells (lanthanides and actinides set aside) | 90 |
| cells the structure admits | 126 |
| **external definition cost E(X)** | **36** |

 The thirty-six are (p1, g2) through (p1, g17), (p2, g3) through (p2, g12), and (p3, g3) through (p3, g12) — **the gaps in the short periods, every one of them.**

 This is not a defect in the periodic table. It is a fact about what the periodic table's coordinates can and cannot carry. Period and group locate an element; they do not encode why period 1 has room for two elements and period 4 for eighteen. That information travels alongside the table, in the schooling of whoever reads it.

![Figure 6.1](figures/figure-6.1.png)

 Figure 6.1. The external definition cost of seven indices. Four are self-defining. The calendar's seven cells are the
 content of Thirty days hath September; the periodic table's thirty-six are the gaps in the short periods.

### 6.1 What "the structure admits" means
 The reconstruction is mechanical. Given a set of cells X on coordinates (x₁, …, x_d), read off two things:

    the value sets Âᵢ(X) = { xᵢ : x ∈ X } — which values occur the bounds φ̂ᵢⱼ(v) = max{ xᵢ : x ∈ X, xⱼ ≤ v
    } — how far one coordinate reaches given another

 and then form

    ℛ(X) = { x ∈ ∏ Âᵢ(X) : xᵢ ≤ φ̂ᵢⱼ(xⱼ) for all i ≠ j }

 No outside knowledge enters. ℛ(X) is what a reader could reconstruct from the cells alone.

 E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X| is the gap: cells the structure implies and the index denies. For the periodic table it is
 36. For Λ, built in the next chapter, it is 0.

![Figure 6.2](figures/figure-6.2.png)

 Figure 6.2. Blue: the ninety cells the table holds. Red: the thirty-six its own coordinates admit and it denies. A reader
 given only the occupied cells would reconstruct all one hundred and twenty-six.

 E is a property of a layout, not of chemistry. Computed on four conventions over the same elements:

 **And the thirty-six decompose, but not as this book has said, and the missing cell is helium's.**
 Recomputed on the drawn eighteen-column layout with all 118 elements:

  real but deferred by the Madelung order — 3d (10),

### 6.2 It is not a peculiarity of chemistry
 The same computation on other indices:

  index                                                       \       X\                          E(X)   self-defining

  a box ordering, l ≥ w ≥ h                                   56      0           yes

  the drawn nuclide band, between drip lines                  383     0           yes

 **The nuclide row names a drawn band and not a measurement, and the distinction is the whole of

 **The measurement is the other object, and it does not close.** Taking the particle-bound nuclides

 **What the nine are is content the coordinates cannot carry.** Be-8 is unbound because it is two

 **And the same shape appears a third time, in chemistry, where it can be watched arriving.** An index

### 6.3 The calendar can be repaired, and the repair is instructive
 The calendar fails for one reason: days(m) is not monotone in m, because February has 28. Relabel the

## 7. The construction of Λ
 Λ is a set of eight-tuples. Each is a transition cell: a source configuration, a target configuration, and the
 electron count moved between them.

      (n, ℓ, k, q, e, f, g, 2S)

| | |
|---|---|
| *n* | source shell |
| ℓ | source subshell |
| *k* | source occupancy |
| *q* | electrons removed |
| *e* | target shell |
| *f* | target subshell |
| *g* | target occupancy |
| 2*S* | multiplicity |

 Five further coordinates — 2S′, v, 2J_c, K and 2J — extend Λ₈ to Λ₁₃ when target spin, seniority and
 angular-momentum coupling are carried explicitly; §12.11 builds the tower and fixes the order, which is
 J_c, then K, then J. Everything in this book that does not concern coupling is stated for Λ₈.

 One row of the table below is not like the others. Three origins — Pauli, the hydrogenic solution,
 counting — yield exact constraints. The fourth, vector coupling, yields an envelope: 2S ≤ k contains
 every physical multiplicity and admits values no k electrons can carry, at 48.5% density at the caps of
 §7.4. §12.11.3 states the dichotomy and §12.11.2 proves it is forced.

### 7.1 The constraints, and where each comes from
 Λ is not all of the eight-fold product. It is the subset satisfying:

  constraint                      origin
  ℓ≤n−1                           hydrogenic radial solution
  k ≤ 2(2ℓ + 1)                   Pauli exclusion
  q≤k                             counting — cannot remove more than are present
  f≤e−1                           hydrogenic radial solution
  g ≤ 2(2f + 1)                   Pauli exclusion
  g≤q                             counting — cannot place more than were removed
  2S ≤ k                          vector coupling

 **Seven constraints, four origins, and nothing else.** No constraint in Λ comes from anywhere but Pauli, the hydrogenic radial solution, counting, or angular-momentum coupling. That exhaustiveness matters in Part III, where it is the reason the object's properties can be attributed to *indexing* rather than to physics smuggled in through a bound.

### 7.2 Every constraint is of one form
 Each constraint reads xᵢ ≤ φ(xⱼ) — one coordinate bounded by a monotone function of one other. None is
 a sum. None is a difference. That is not an accident of presentation; Chapter 17 shows that a sum could
 not appear here, because a set cut out by a sum bound is not closed.

 **Consequence, developed in Chapter 8:** the graph whose nodes are coordinates and whose edges are constraints is a **tree**.

![Figure 7.1](figures/figure-7.1.png)

 Figure 7.1. Every constraint binds one coordinate to one other. Eight nodes, seven edges, connected — a tree, and
 therefore treewidth 1. Three results in this book follow from that fact alone.

### 7.3 Λ is closed
 For any two cells x, y ∈ Λ, both x ∨ y and x ∧ y — the coordinatewise maximum and minimum — are again
 in Λ.

 *Proof.* Each constraint is *xᵢ* ≤ φ(*xⱼ*) with φ non-decreasing. Suppose (*x*∨*y*)ᵢ = *xᵢ*. Then

    (x∨y)ᵢ = xᵢ ≤ φ(xⱼ) ≤ φ(max(xⱼ, yⱼ)) = φ((x∨y)ⱼ)

 by monotonicity. Meets are symmetric. ∎

 And E(Λ) = 0, verified by direct computation at four cap settings — 216, 976, 1,636 and 2,394 cells —
 exact in one step and stable under a second application of ℛ.

## 8. What Λ is — distributive, modular, Sperner


 **The standing convention, stated once so it need not be repeated.** Every figure in this book that
 depends on the caps is computed at **(n_max, e_max, ℓ_max, k_max, f_max) = (3, 3, 1, 3, 1)** unless the
 section names others. Where a figure is recomputed under variation the settings are printed beside it,
 as at §6.2.1, §12.11.1.1, §12.11.1.2 and §22.1.1.1.

    **A cap-dependent figure without a stated cap is not thereby unqualified — it is at these
    caps.** What would be a defect is a figure at *other* caps that does not say so, and audit 10
    checks for that.

 The convention was in force from the first page and had never been written down: 84 paragraphs carry a
 cap-dependent figure and 69 of them name no cap, which is 82% relying on a rule the book did not state.
 **§32.4.2's distinction is why this matters** — every one of those 69 carries a *value* rather than an
 identity, and a value without its setting is a reading whose conditions are missing. Register 395.

### 8.1 Distributive
 Λ is a sublattice of a product of chains, and every such sublattice is distributive. Verified on 4,000
 randomly drawn triples, no failures.

 This is the least surprising fact in the chapter and the most load-bearing: it is what admits Birkhoff's representation, which is the next section.

### 8.2 Rank is conserved
 Λ has a conservation law, and it is exact.

    rank(a ∨ b) + rank(a ∧ b) = rank(a) + rank(b)

 **Verified on all 475,800 pairs: zero violations.**

 **This is modularity, and it is strictly stronger than what most rank functions satisfy.** Matroid rank is *sub*modular — the left side is ≤ the right. Entropy is submodular. **Λ's rank is modular, with equality, and that equality is the signature of distributivity.**

### 8.2.1 What it means
 Join and meet redistribute rank without creating or destroying it. Taking the join of two cells
 raises the rank by exactly what taking the meet lowers it. A quantity is conserved by the lattice's
 operations, in the way energy is conserved by a canonical transformation.

 **The question came from outside the subject.** Celestial mechanics is organised around invariants — the Jacobi integral, angular momentum, energy — and asking *what does Λ conserve* is not a question a spectroscopist would think to put. **This book had not put it.**

### 8.2.2 And it is a cheaper test than §8.1's
 §8.1 verifies distributivity by checking a ∧ (b ∨ c) = (a∧b) ∨ (a∧c) over triples — O(n³).
 Modularity of rank is a pairwise condition, O(n²), and on a graded lattice with this rank function it is
 equivalent:

| test | sample | time |
|---|---|---|
| distributive law, triples | 4,000 | 0.0375 s |
| **modular rank, pairs** | 4,000 | **0.0188 s** |

 **Both true. The second is the one to run first**, because a failure of modularity is a failure of distributivity and it is found in half the work.

### 8.3 Seventeen generators
 By Birkhoff's theorem, a finite distributive lattice is the lattice of down-sets of its poset of join-irreducibles.
 For Λ at caps (3,3,1,3), k ≥ 1:

    976 cells ← 17 join-irreducibles, 20 covering relations

 and the correspondence is exact: **all 976 down-sets of the 17-element poset are precisely the 976 cells.** A fifty-seven-fold compression.

 **The covering relations are the physics made visible:**

| cover | reads |
|---|---|
| *e*=2 ⋖ *e*=2, *f*=1 | a target subshell requires its shell |
| *k*=2 ⋖ *k*=2, *q*=2 | you may remove what you have |
| *n*=2 ⋖ *n*=2, ℓ=1 ⋖ *n*=2, ℓ=1, *k*=3 | shell before subshell before occupancy |

 **And the shape is cap-independent.** Across six settings from 976 to 27,873 cells the generator count grows — 17, 23, 31, 32 — while the *patterns* hold at **fifteen, with zero new and zero lost.** Only multiplicities change.

 That is what licenses stating the poset once.

![Figure 8.1](figures/figure-8.1.png)

 Figure 8.1. The seventeen join-irreducibles and their twenty covering relations. Every one of the 976 cells is a down-set
 of this poset, and every down-set is a cell — a fifty-seven-fold compression, exact. The covers are the constraints of §7.1
 made visible: shell before subshell before occupancy, and a target subshell requiring its shell.

### 8.4 Sperner, and not symmetric
 The largest antichain in Λ equals its largest rank level — the Sperner property — verified exactly at five
 cap settings by Dilworth's theorem and bipartite matching, no exceptions. At caps (3,3,1,3), k ≥ 1 the maximum
 is 122 at rank 11.

 The rank sequence is **log-concave**, hence unimodal, which is why Sperner holds rather than merely happening to.

 **But Λ is not rank-symmetric**, so it has **no symmetric chain decomposition** and the classical result for divisor lattices does not transfer. The asymmetry is itself a measurement:

    centre of mass 11.07 against midpoint 11.5 — skew −0.43, computed from the full rank sequence
    at caps (3,3,1,3), k ≥ 1, over all 976 cells

 Low ranks are cut by floors (*n* ≥ 1, *k* ≥ 1, *e* ≥ 1); high ranks by caps (ℓ ≤ *n*−1, *k* ≤ 2(2ℓ+1), *q* ≤ *k*, *g* ≤ *q*). **There are more caps than floors, so the top is pruned harder.** The skew is how much more Pauli constrains than counting does.

 Nor is Λ self-dual. Only 8 of 976 cells survive the reflection x ↦ max − x, coordinate by coordinate —
 reproduced exactly on recomputation. The tower session's competing figure of 112 was computed under
 x ↦ max + min − x, a different map, which the floors n ≥ 1, k ≥ 1, e ≥ 1 separate from this one; under
 that map 112 cells have their image in Λ and none is fixed. Both counts are right about their own
 reflection. The discrepancy was definitional, and it is closed. This reflection is not decoration: restricted to
 one occupancy coordinate it is particle-hole conjugation, terms(ℓᵏ) = terms(ℓ^(4ℓ+2−k)) exactly, and
 §12.11.2 shows it is one of the three machines that price every coupling axis. The
 two sides of the object are genuinely distinguishable, which Chapter 12 develops.

![Figure 8.2](figures/figure-8.2.png)

 Figure 8.2. The rank sequence over all 976 cells is log-concave, hence unimodal, hence Sperner. It is not symmetric: the
 centre of mass sits below the midpoint by 0.43, because Λ has more caps than floors.

### 8.5 The constraint graph is a tree
 Eight coordinates, seven constraints, connected:

    e — f — g — q — k — ℓ — n, with 2S attached to k

 **Treewidth 1.** Three consequences run through the rest of the book:

 **The void needs no sieve.** A tree has no cycles, so there is nothing for inclusion–exclusion to correct. Chapter 10 gives the closed-form count.

 **The order is recoverable.** Chapter 15 recovers Λ's coordinate orders from an unlabelled bag of cells by propagation along this tree — 20 of 20.

 **And the constraint graph offers no redundancy.** There is exactly one path between any two nodes. So the two-route protection of Chapter 16 cannot come from the constraints; it must come from derived quantities. **That is a real constraint on how the object defends itself, and it is visible here, three chapters early.**

### 8.6 Order dimension

### 10.1 What the void is made of

 **And Λ already carries time, in the only form a transition can carry it.** The source end is a

### 11.1.1 A seventh, in binary, and it earns its place
 Asked whether binary belongs among the languages, the answer is that it does, and the book's own

    **binary** — Λ is the set of 976 words in {0,1}¹⁷ that are down-sets of the generator poset
    A.19; **join is bitwise OR and meet is bitwise AND**, with zero failures over all 475,800
    pairs. The map cell ↦ word is a bijection.

 The seventeen bits are the seventeen generators. Birkhoff's correspondence, which §8.3 states and A.19

 bit-string. Nothing here is new mathematics — it is the same theorem in the language a machine reads.

 **What it distinguishes, and why the other six cannot.** *Logic* gives χ, a predicate that tests

    bits carried per cell                 17

    surplus                             7.07 bits per cell

 **A bit is a generator.** Bit *i* is set in a cell's word exactly when generator *i* of A.19 lies

 **And the bits are not free of one another.** The twenty covering relations of J(Λ) are twenty

 bit *i* set. **Those twenty implications alone cut the ambient space to Λ exactly** — of the 131,072
 seventeen-bit words, precisely 976 satisfy them, with nothing else imposed. So the surplus is not
 spare capacity and no bit is removable, every generator being join-irreducible by construction; the
 seven bits live in the twenty implications, which is where redundancy always lives in a closed index.

 **And in that language Λ is a circuit, which fixes what kind of machine this book is.** The
 seventeen generators are input lines; the twenty implications are gates; join is OR and meet is AND.
 Computed: the twenty gates alone accept **976 words of the 131,072 available, which is exactly Λ**, at
 a depth of five. Available: AND, OR, implication. Absent: NOT, feedback, memory.

    **Λ₈ is a monotone boolean circuit. It decides membership; it does not compute a function of
    successive inputs.**

 **P20 already said this and used another vocabulary.** It states that monotone two-variable bounds
 *close always in one pass*, where full arithmetic never closes by Gödel. Closing in one pass is
 constant depth, and constant depth is combinational — **P20 was a classification of this object's
 computational power before anything had been counted.** §32.4.1 says the same from the third side:
 no negation, so no self-referential contradiction, so no loop to diverge in.

 **And the ninth axis is where it stops being static.** §12.11.0 shows Λ₉ closed under composition —

## 12. The shape — a cylinder over the transfer

### 12.1 A cylinder, not a Möbius band
 Λ's derived quantities fall into two classes:

| **ascending** — rise up a series | **descending** — fall up a series |
|---|---|
| *e*, ν, *V* | *T*, *r*, δ, spacing, *w* |

 exchanged under ν ↦ ν⁻³.

 **The sign structure is bipartite**, and a bipartite structure can never produce an odd number of orientation reversals. Verified exhaustively: **zero reversing loops among all cycles of length 3 to 5.**

    Λ is orientable. It is a cylinder.

 That is a *reason*, not an absence. And both alternative routes to a Möbius band close: a non-monotone quantity has **undefined** edges rather than reversing ones; a quantity independent of ν has **no** edge. There is no third option.

### 12.2 "Over ν", not "graded by ν"
 ν grades every chain of Λ. It grades Λ itself nowhere — 24 of 70 comparable pairs have ν decreasing.

 **That near-miss is the structure in one sentence.** The bracket of Part V operates along chains *because that is exactly where ν is a grading.*

 The name follows: **the Lach Cylinder — a hydrogenic cylinder over ν, and over the transfer.** Not *graded by*. *Over.*

### 12.3 One scale, and one exception
 Height goes as ν⁻², the metric as ν⁻³, and the only linearly rising quantity in the entire structure is

 10⁻¹⁶.

 Λ *decomposes* ν and gains dimension; the bound lattice *recomposes* it and sheds dimension. **Two sides of one object, not two passes over it.**

### 12.5 What Λ is a property of
 Λ is a property of the hydrogenic limit. δ — the quantum defect — is the entire remainder.

    Prediction lives only in the remainder.

 Which is why perfecting the index moves nothing, and why that is a theorem rather than a disappointment. Part III proves it; Part V measures what is left.

 **And §25.6 will sharpen this into its final form.** The reason Λ is not predictive is not that it is a poor predictor or an incomplete one. **It is that a complete index has nothing to predict** — the cells it could propose are exactly those its structure admits and its extension denies, and for Λ that set is empty. **Completeness and predictiveness are alternatives.**

### 12.11.0 Transitions compose, and the ninth axis is what lets them

 **The ninth axis supplies it.** 2S′ ≤ g gives the target its own multiplicity, and the target end

    Define b ∘ a when a's target equals b's source: the composite runs a's source to b's target,
    transferring min(q_a, q_b) — no more than was taken, no more than arrives.

 **Λ₉ is closed under composition, exhaustively: 41,682 composable pairs, zero failures**, and
 associative on 8,434 sampled triples with none. Λ₉ is therefore not merely a lattice of transitions

### 12.11.0.4 The separation hypothesis, named
 Four families of result in this book hold *because the constraint graph is a tree*, and none of them
 says so. The factorising count, the recoverability of the order, the balance at a cut and the
 propagation of Chapter 15 all use it; §7.1 records treeness as a fact about Λ and never as a
 condition. **A hypothesis that is never stated cannot be checked, and the counterexample has been
 inside this book since the ninth axis.**

 **Λ₉′ is the test, and it separates the results.** Adding 2S′ ≤ 2f+1 closes the cycle f — g — 2S′ — f

  closure, E(X) = 0                               0              **0**
  factorisation over the transfer, defect         0              **0**

    being conditioned. Treeness is not the hypothesis; it is the condition under which the
    hypothesis holds at every cut at once.**

### 12.11.0.12 How an index enters a larger index, and what it looks like from there

 requires the larger index to be built.

 lattice, so the only chain-valued function ℛ accepts on it is its rank. 199,130 cells become **44
 rank values**: 17.60 bits collapse to 5.46, a compression of 4,526 to 1, with **12.14 bits per cell
 lost.** Thirty-one per cent of the object survives the promotion and the rest is not representable as
 a coordinate at all. Structurally the result is the same kind of thing as dimension 1 of Λ, which is a
 chain of three — so an index can be an axis of another, at that price.

 **A coarse coordinate is a branching node.** At Λ₉ the rank chain has 21 values and the fibres beneath
 them run from 1 cell to **185**. One point above stands for up to a hundred and eighty-five below, and
 nothing in the coordinate distinguishes them.

 pairs, closed and associative. Reduced to rank there are 264 distinct (rank a, rank b) inputs, and
 **only 17% of them determine a single output rank.** The worst spread is **twelve** possible output
 ranks from one input pair; the composite's rank lies in [3, 23], narrowed by the inputs and not fixed
 by them.

 Twice the title has changed, and both changes record findings rather than preferences.

 The book was called The Lach Index Lattice until its shape was computed. The shape is a cylinder
 over the transfer, so the object's name became The Lach Cylinder — and §13.2 gives the reason.

 Then the register outgrew the object. By the end there were one thousand five hundred and sixty-one
 withdrawals, twenty-five prime audits, twenty principles and twenty-four protocols — and the demonstration

 **And a third time, when the languages were gathered.** Fifty sections across fourteen chapters made
 a claim about language and none owned one; Part IV now does, and §21.1 shows that eight results
 already in this book are one statement — **a language is a coordinate system, translation is
 re-coordinatisation, and E is what the translation costs.** The subtitle records it.

    **The Lach Cylinder — a closed index of transitions, and the languages they speak**

 **Three things changed and each is a finding.** *Closed* replaces nothing and adds the theorem:
 E(Λ) = 0, verified at 976 cells in six languages. *The languages they speak* replaces *closure,
 self-reference, refusal, and the price of certainty* — four terms that named four Parts, where the
 new clause names what the Parts have in common.

 **And the grammar is the claim.** Not *the languages it is spoken in*, which would make the index

      The title is now The Method, and The Lach Cylinder is its subtitle.

# PART III — THE LAW

## 14. Closure
 A set is closed when nothing its own structure admits is missing from it.

### 14.1 The characterisation
 Theorem 14.1 (A.2). X is closed iff X = ℛ(X), where ℛ reconstructs value sets and pairwise monotone
 bounds from X's own extension.

 **This is not new mathematics and the book gains by saying so.** A.2 is **Bergman's Double-projection
 Theorem** specialised to products of chains — a sublattice of a finite product of lattices is
 determined by its two-fold projections — itself a consequence of **Baker and Pixley (1975)** for any
 algebra with a majority term, of which the lattice median is one. Λ's coordinates are counts, so each
 factor is a chain, and a sublattice of a product of two chains is exactly a staircase cut by monotone
 bounds, which is what ℛ recovers as φ_ij. The proof in §16.1 is correct and fifty years late.

 **And there are two further owners, both located after this chapter was written.** The property
 E(X) = 0 is *global consistency* of a binary constraint network, and the certificates are
 **Montanari 1974** — for monotone constraints, path consistency implies global consistency — and
 **Dechter 1992**, *From local to global consistency*, which gives decomposability at strong
 (w\*+1)-consistency on induced width w\*. **Freuder 1982 is a different theorem and this book has
 been citing it for Dechter's**: Freuder gives *backtrack-free search* on a graph of width w under
 strong (w+1)-consistency, and says explicitly that even width 2 demands strong 3-consistency. The
 mis-citation is corrected here and recorded at register 400.

 **And the constraint class has a name.** A binary constraint that is (α, β)-monotone with
 α, β ∈ {≤, ≥} is a **staircase** constraint, and the connected row-convex class containing it is
 closed under composition, intersection and transposition — **Deville, Barták and Van Hentenryck,
 *Artificial Intelligence* 1999**. φ̂ recovers exactly a staircase, so the operator of §6.1 has been
 building a named object since Chapter 6. Register 401.

 **What follows is that E(Λ) = 0 is the discovery that Λ is a sublattice**, and sublattices have been
 binary-determined since 1975. The development is at A.2; the register carries the finding at 224.

### 14.2 R is a closure operator
 Extensive, monotone, idempotent — 150 of 150 on all three axioms.

 So E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X| is a closure defect, a standard object in Galois theory, formal concept analysis
 and database dependency theory.

 **This book claims no novelty for the machinery.** What is offered is the application: computing the closure defect of an *index*, and finding that the periodic table's is 36 while Λ's is 0.

### 14.3 The scope, stated exactly
 Theorem 14.1 requires each coordinate to be presented as a chain. That is not the same as requiring the
 factors to be chains: any distributive factor can be so presented, by Birkhoff, as the down-sets of its
 join-irreducibles — one chain per irreducible.

 What fails is bundling. ℛ reconstructs coordinate by coordinate, so folding two chains into one
 non-chain coordinate hides structure from it. In tests, the same sets presented bundled and presented
 decomposed both gave 80/80 agreement — the theorem survives, but only when the presentation
 respects it.

### 14.4 The three consequences
 Closure yields three properties, developed in the next three chapters:

### 14.5 The family of all closed sets

 A closed index is one object. **The closed subsets of a closed index are a family**, and this book
 has carried the question of what that family is since Λ was built. It is answerable by enumeration
 at small size, and the answer is standard once it is seen.

  ambient        cells   closed subsets   of 2ⁿ    ∩ closed   ∪ closed
  2 × 2 × 2          8       **73**       28.5%     **100%**     64.4%
  3 × 3              9      **146**       28.5%     **100%**     68.3%
  2 × 2 × 2 × 2     16      **731**        1.1%     **100%**     32.6%

    **The closed sets of ℛ form a MOORE FAMILY: closed under intersection, containing
    the whole index, and NOT closed under union.**

 That is the standard fact about any closure operator — the closed sets of a closure operator are a
 Moore family, and the correspondence between operators, families and lattices is cryptomorphic. **It
 is worth stating here because the asymmetry is ℛ's own, one level up.** ℛ carries meets and refuses
 joins in §14.2; its family of fixed points does the same, at 100% against 32–68%.

 **And it is the setting in which register 458's finding lives.** Λ₉ is closed and 300 of 300 random
 subsets of it are open, because the closed ones are a Moore family inside a power set — a vanishing
 minority, and the only place from which the open ones can be measured.

 **The count for Λ itself is open.** Brute force is 2⁹⁷⁶. The Moore-family structure gives the route,
 since a Moore family is determined by its meet-irreducible members, and §8.4 already counts those
 for Λ under a different name. Q item R. Register 461.

 **And the FAMILY is examined at §14.6**, where it is shown to be open — every member closed,
 the family not — which is why counting it for Λ is a question about an object that cannot be stated
 rather than one that is merely large.

### 14.5.1 Λ is the closure of seven cells

 The meet-irreducibles are the route, and taking it turns up a property of Λ that had not been
 looked for.

 **First, no cell of Λ is removable.** ℛ(Λ \ {x}) = Λ for **every one of the 976 cells** — remove any
 single cell and the operator puts it back, exactly, adding one. So Λ has no closed set of the form
 Λ \ {x}, and its meet-irreducibles are not coatoms. **Every cell is implied by the other 975.**

 **Second, and this is the number.** Greedy removal while ℛ still returns Λ, three independent
 shuffles: **12, 11, 12 cells.**

    **Λ is the closure of SEVEN of its cells — a compression of 139 to 1, exactly.**

 *This section read "at most ten" and before that "eleven", both from greedy removal. §14.5.9 gives
 seven, exact by branch and bound, and §2.24 is the protocol that failure earned.*

 *Greedy removal gives an upper bound, not a minimum; §14.5.6 records the spread across shuffles and both operators.*

 That is tighter than Birkhoff's seventeen join-irreducibles, and for a stated reason: ℛ fills the
 envelope box where the lattice join reaches only the down-set. **The generating set is smaller than
 the generating set of the lattice**, because ℛ is the stronger operator.

 **What the small ambients say about the family.** Meet-irreducible closed sets number 12, 14 and 20
 at 8, 9 and 16 cells — about 1.25 per cell — and they generate the whole family under intersection
 exactly, once the empty set is counted among the closed. **Linear in the index, where the family
 they generate is not.**

 **And the quantity has a name outside this book.** In a convexity space the **Carathéodory number**
 is the least c such that anything in the hull of U lies in the hull of some S ⊆ U with |S| ≤ c, and
 it equals the largest irredundant set. For a semilattice with its subsemilattices as convex sets —
 which is Λ's case — the Helly number is the height and the **Carathéodory number is the breadth**.
 **This book already cites Helly and has never cited Carathéodory**, which is the second bibliography
 gap the cycle's step 2 has found in two runs. Registers 466–468.

### 14.6.1 Why it cannot be stated

 (ii) is the whole of it. **Meet is intersection and stays inside the family at 100%. Join is not
 union**, which escapes at a third to two thirds, and must be closed back in. **So there is no
 operation on this family that leads out of it, and the one that would leads nowhere at all.**

 **And §14.5.7 says what that costs.** A closed index has a seed — Λ's is seven cells for
 976. **An open index has none**; the best available is
 seed(ℛ(X)) + E, and here E is 64,804 at an ambient of sixteen. **The property that makes an index
 printable is exactly what this object lacks, and it lacks it more the larger the ambient grows.**

    **This is the one index whose cost of statement exceeds its content — and it is the
    family every other index in this book belongs to.**

 **What is NOT claimed.** That this family is a dimension, a level, or a place. §16.6 grades
 *multiverse dimension* ⅅ_gro — a term with no referent established anywhere — and §29.2.2 records it
 as not posable. **The theorem needs none of that**, and its three clauses are each a computation on
 a finite ambient. Registers 509–510.

### 15.1 S1 — the alphabet
    Âᵢ(X) = { xᵢ : x ∈ X }

 A projection. **Always succeeds, no conditions.**

### 15.2 S3 — the bounds
    φ̂ᵢⱼ(v) = max{ xᵢ : x ∈ X, xⱼ ≤ v }

 **Corollary, and it is what makes §2.23 a requirement rather than a preference.** A closed index
 satisfies X = ℛ(X), which by the definition of ℛ means

    X = { x ∈ ∏ᵢ Âᵢ(X) : xᵢ ≤ φ̂ᵢⱼ(xⱼ) for all i ≠ j }

 — **the envelope set determines the index completely.** So the shape of a closed index is its
 envelopes, and S3 says the envelopes are recoverable from the cells. **Every closed index is
 therefore expressible, and the expression is always already present in what it prints.** Stating it

 Read off the cells. For Λ₈ that is 56 functions, all recovered, and ℛ(Λ) = Λ exactly. Always succeeds

### 15.3 S2 — the order, which is the hard one
 Given the alphabet but not the ordering of its values, can the ordering be recovered?

 **The necessary condition is provable and dimension-free.** Say *u* **may precede** *v* on axis *i* if, for every *p* in the fibre over *u* and every *q* in the fibre over *v*, the meet lies in F(*u*) and the join in F(*v*).

    Lemma. If X is closed and u < v on axis i, then u may precede v. Proof. Take x with xᵢ = u and y with
    yᵢ = v. Then x ∧ y has i-coordinate u, so its other coordinates lie in F(u); and x ∨ y has i-coordinate v,
    so its other coordinates lie in F(v). ∎ Nothing in the argument uses d = 2.

 **At *d* = 2 the converse also holds** and the criterion is exact: X is closed under some order iff "may precede" is a total order, and that order **is** the relabelling. Verified on 120 sets; 274 of 274 constructed total orders give closed sets.

 Above d = 2 the converse fails. Being a total order on every axis separately is necessary and not
 sufficient — the axes' requirements can be mutually incompatible. That is developed in §18.4, because it
 is a limitation rather than a mechanism.

### 15.4 What does work above d = 2: propagation along the tree
 If the constraint graph is a tree, each axis is constrained only by its parent. Root anywhere, fix the
 root by brute force, and extend with backtracking.

    Λ's orders are recovered from a scrambled bag of cells: 20 of 20, at two cap settings, on 216
    and 976 cells with all eight axes independently permuted.

 **Cost Σᵢ|Aᵢ|!, never the product ∏ᵢ|Aᵢ|!.**

 Two earlier methods failed on the same task, and the failures are instructive. Alternating refinement across all eight axes at once: **0 of 12.** Greedy propagation without backtracking: 42% and 25%. **The tree says only neighbours interact; a method that ignores that recovers nothing.**

 The unqualified claim — the index contains its own definition — holds for Λ because its constraint graph is

## 16. Self-defence — data, derivation, totality

### 16.1 The counting argument
 Let p be the parameters an index assigns and q = Φ(p) the quantities derived from them.

    ⅅ = dim q − rank ∂Φ/∂p ≥ dim q − dim p

 *Proof.* The Jacobian is dim *q* × dim *p*; its rank exceeds neither. ∎

 **Verified on seven dimension pairs and 420 random nonlinear maps.** No closure required, no smoothness beyond differentiability.

    Corollary. dim q > dim p ⇒ ⅅ ≥ 1.

 ⅅ counts functionally independent relations the derived quantities must satisfy. Each is a test the index
 must pass. For Λ with p = (T, n, Z, σ) and q = (ν, δ, V, r, w, e), rank is 4 and ⅅ = 2, spanned by

    (a) V = 4ν/3 (b) w = V · e

### 16.2 The split, and it is canonical
 (a) holds under the Rydberg law and fails under power-4, exponential and logarithmic laws. (b) holds
 under all four.

 **Tested under four unrelated perturbations, verdicts identical.** The split is not an artefact of which law one chooses to vary.

 **A widened bound on a variable with descendants forces theirs to widen too**, so the fibre undercounts in proportion to how much of the tree sits downstream. **Leaves are exact; the root is off by a factor of 2.5.**

### 16.8.5 Nothing can be removed, and the floor is derived rather than measured
 §16.8.4 prices insertion. Removal has a floor, and it is not zero anywhere.

 **Pushback.** For a cell x, count the pairs of *other* cells that produce it — J(x) joining to x, M(x)
 meeting at x. Remove x and that is exactly how many pairs of survivors fail. Over all 475,800 pairs
 of Λ₈:

  minimum over all 976 cells                    **16**
  median                                        504
  maximum                                       5,091
  mean                                          739
  cells removable with no failing pair          **0**

 **No cell of Λ₈ can leave without the remainder contradicting the removal**, and the weakest is
 implied back sixteen ways.

 **The floor is not a measurement.** A cell with pushback zero would have to be join-prime *and*
 meet-prime — irreducible on both sides. Λ₈ has eighteen of each and **their intersection is empty**,
 at every cap tested. So zero is unreachable by construction, not by luck.

 **And the minimum that *can* leave follows from the same fact.**

    **X ∖ [a, b] is a sublattice if and only if a is join-prime and b is meet-prime.**

 *Proof.* Let R = [a,b] and suppose z ∈ R with z = x ∨ y and x, y ∉ R. Since x, y ≤ z ≤ b, being
 outside R means x ≱ a and y ≱ a, while a ≤ x ∨ y. In a distributive lattice every join-irreducible is
 join-prime, so a ≤ x ∨ y forces a ≤ x or a ≤ y — contradiction. Conversely if a is join-reducible,
 a = u ∨ v with u, v < a, both under b and neither above a, so u, v ∉ R while u ∨ v = a ∈ R. Dually for
 meets and b. ∎

 Computed at the book's caps: **step(Λ₈) = 4**, the interval running (2,1,3,3,2,1,3,0) to
 (3,1,3,3,3,1,3,0) — a box free in exactly two coordinates, **n and e, the two shell coordinates and
 the two ends of the caterpillar**. Removing it leaves 972 cells with **zero join or meet failures
 across all 471,906 surviving pairs.**

 **The pushback floor of 16 and the step of 4 are one fact seen twice.** Both say: there is no cell
 whose removal the rest of the index does not contradict, because there is no cell irreducible on both
 sides. Register 349.
